title: High-Frequency Exponential-Utility Maximization under Fractional Brownian Motion

p.t: Fractional Brownian motion with Hurst parameter H ∈ (0, 1) is a continuous, zero-mean Gaussian process B H = (B H t ) t≥0 such that The process B H is self-similar, satisfies B H at d = a H B H t , and has stationary increments. Moreover, the successive increments of B H are positively correlated for H > 1/2, negatively correlated for H < 1/2, while H = 1/2 recovers the usual Brownian motion with independent increments. Fractional Brownian motion, which can display the long-range dependence observed in empirical data when H > 1/2 (see [3,9,14] and the references therein), is not a semimartingale when H ̸ = 1 2 and so, in the frictionless case it leads to arbitrage opportunities (see, for instance, [10,2]). If trading is restricted to a discrete trading grid, arbitrage opportunities disappear. This short note was inspired by [6] where the authors study high-frequency trading in a market in which the asset price is driven by fractional Brownian motion. They derive explicit locally mean-variance optimal trading strategies for a fixed trading frequency and analyze their behavior as the trading frequency tends to infinity. In this note, we provide an analogous analysis for exponential utility maximization. We consider a discretized version of the fBm framework. Namely, we fix a time horizon T > 0, n ∈ N, and consider a financial market that is active at times 0, T n , 2T n , . . . , T . The financial market consists of a savings account, which for simplicity bears no interest, and a risky asset S = B H . The investor's flow of information is given by the filtration F kT n := σ S 0 , S T n , . . . , S kT n , k = 0, 1, . . . , n.

A trading strategy is a random vector γ = γ iT n n-1 i=0 that is adapted to the above filtration. Denote by A n the set of all trading strategies. For γ ∈ A n , the corresponding portfolio value at the maturity date is given by The investor's preferences are described by the exponential utility function u(x) = -exp(-αx), x ∈ R, with absolute risk-aversion parameter α > 0, and her goal is to ( 1.1) maximize E [-exp (-αV γ T )] over γ ∈ A n . Clearly, for any trading strategy γ and any constant λ ∈ R, V λγ T = λV γ T . Thus, without loss of generality, we set the risk-aversion parameter to α = 1. Moreover, by the self-similarity of fractional Brownian motion, we may also assume, without loss of generality, that T = 1. Next, before we formulate our main results we need some preparations.
